sources.news_title: "I'll Say It's Not Good": Trump Refers to the Alleged Cyber Attack on an FBI Database
sources.text:
"Diré que no es bueno": Trump se refiere al supuesto ciberataque a una base de datos del FBI
Donald Trump se refirió este sábado 21 de noviembre al supuesto ciberataque que sufrió el FBI contra su Centro Nacional de Información Criminal, pero matizó que el hecho puede servir para obtener información valiosa que de otro modo no se habría conocido.
"Acabamos de enterarnos y diré que no es bueno. No me gusta, pero quizá aprendamos cosas que nunca habríamos sabido de otra manera", dijo el mandatario Donald Trump en declaraciones al canal 'Fox News'.
El viernes, la cadena 'CNN'' informó que el FBI estaba investigando una presunta violación de una base de datos nacional utilizada por agencias policiales federales, estatales y locales para compartir información sobre justicia penal.
El Centro Nacional de Información Criminal, conocido como NCIC, es una base de datos informatizada de información sobre justicia penal a la que tienen acceso los organismos policiales locales, estatales y federales, e incluye registros sobre fugitivos, personas desaparecidas, antecedentes penales, bienes robados y otros temas.
La noticia de que el NCIC fue blanco de un ataque tiene lugar en un momento en que el país ha experimentado una serie de interrupciones digitales en el sector público y privado que, según funcionarios de la Administración Trump, fueron causadas por esfuerzos regulares para actualizar los sistemas informáticos y corregir vulnerabilidades, y no por un ciberataque.
Trump afirmó sobre el caso este sábado que siempre intenta buscar "un enfoque positivo" y vinculó una eventual filtración de datos con las investigaciones y polémicas que marcaron su carrera política, a las que volvió a referirse como "engaños".
"Estaba el engaño de Rusia; todos esos otros engaños; lo que llamamos el engaño de Ucrania. Todo aquello de la llamada telefónica, la llamada perfecta, como yo digo. Hay muchas otras cosas y quizá sepamos más al respecto. Quizá sepamos sobre el fraude electoral, todo el fraude electoral que tuvo lugar", aludió.
Sin embargo, no aclaró cómo se produjo el acceso, quiénes estarían detrás del ataque ni si los intrusos consiguieron extraer información de la base de datos.
El incidente se produce después de que en septiembre el FBI investigara un presunto robo de datos confidenciales de empleados y aspirantes a trabajar en la agencia, tras una denuncia del grupo de ciberdelincuentes ShinyHunters sobre una intrusión en el portal de empleo.
Estados Unidos ha vivido una oleada de fallos de servicios informáticos en varias de sus entidades públicas y empresas en las últimas semanas, aunque el Gobierno de Trump las ha descartado, negando que exista un ataque sistémico por parte de agentes externos.
En medio de la crisis, el director nacional de ciberseguridad, Sean Cairncross, fue relevado el jueves de su puesto por la Casa Blanca y sustituido de manera interina por la hasta ahora directora de información del Pentágono, Kirsten Davies.
Con AP y EFE

sources.news_title: Trump downplays FBI data breach of NCIC, adds 'positive spin'
sources.text:
Trump downplays FBI data breach of NCIC, adds 'positive spin'
Summary
Hackers reportedly breached the FBI’s National Crime Information Center, a law-enforcement database used across the United States, and President Donald Trump downplayed the incident Saturday. Trump called the breach “not good” but said it might help reveal information, including what he described as voter fraud. The FBI has not confirmed the breach. A former FBI official warned that hackers could potentially affect the accuracy of information officers rely on for public safety.
Key Facts
- The NCIC contains FBI fingerprint records and information on wanted persons, violent felons and missing persons.
- The database is restricted to law enforcement but is not classified.
- CNN and NBC reported the breach Friday night, citing the incident; the FBI had not confirmed it.
- The USDA told employees that a system used to facilitate payments to farmers was targeted in a cyberattack, NBC reported Friday.
An FBI database that police all over the country use was hacked in the second major security breach in two months, and President Donald Trump downplayed it Saturday.
The FBI's National Crime Information Center, which police use constantly, was hacked, CNN and NBC reported Friday night. The NCIC includes FBI fingerprint records, wanted persons, violent felons, missing persons and related information. Its use is restricted to law enforcement but is not classified.
On Saturday, Trump said the breach is "not good," but that it could be helpful to him.
We could "learn things that we would have never learned otherwise," he said.
"I always like to put things in a positive spin," Trump said during a phone interview with Fox News when asked about the reports.
"You had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax. You had all of these other hoaxes. We call it Ukraine, the Ukraine, Ukraine, Ukraine hoax ... the perfect phone call, as I say," Trump said, talking about the call in 2019 when Trump asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to investigate President Joe Biden, while he was running for office.
"You have so many other things. And maybe we'll learn about them," Trump said, pivoting back to the FBI hack. "Maybe we'll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place."
The breach hasn't been confirmed by the FBI or the president.
"Every day, officers across the country rely on NCIC to identify wanted fugitives, check for outstanding warrants and access information that can directly impact officer and public safety," a former FBI official who has led investigations into cybercriminal groups told CNN. "My concern isn't simply whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on."
The USDA told employees that a system used to facilitate payments to farmers was targeted in a cyberattack, NBC reported on Friday.

sources.news_title: ‘Not good’: Trump reacts to FBI hack
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said Saturday that he hoped something good would come from the latest breach of an FBI database.
“I always like to put things on a positive spin,” Trump said in an interview with Fox News.
A sensitive FBI database was hacked in the second major cyber breach for the bureau in two months, two people familiar with the matter told MS NOW.
This time, hackers accessed the National Criminal Information Center, a database that includes FBI fingerprint records, wanted persons, violent felons, missing persons and related information. The database is restricted to law enforcement use but not classified.
It’s unclear how much data was extracted. The FBI did not respond to a request for comment. The hack was first reported by CNN.
Asked about reports of the breach in a Saturday call with Fox News, Trump said he hoped it would shed light on the FBI’s Russia investigation or on “voter fraud.”
“I will say that it’s not good. I don’t like that. But maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise, because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.
“Maybe we’ll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place,” Trump added.

OAN Staff Katherine Mosack
10:45 AM – Saturday, November 21, 2026
President Donald Trump has described the reported breach experienced by the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s (FBI’s) National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database as “not good.”
Reports that the FBI was investigating a breach began to surface across multiple news outlets on Friday night, citing unnamed officials familiar with the matter.
Asked by Fox News’ Kayleigh McEnany — Trump’s former White House Press Secretary — about the purported FBI breach, the president said, “We just heard about it, and I will say that it’s not good, I don’t like that.”
Noting his affinity for putting “a positive spin” on things, Trump mused over the possibility of the breach leading to new releases of information about the Russia collusion investigation of 2016 and the suspected voter fraud in 2020.
“But maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise. You had the Russia Russia Russia hoax, you had all these other hoaxes,” Trump said.
He added, “Maybe we’ll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place.”
The NCIC contains a nationwide criminal information database managed by the FBI’s Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) that’s used by federal, state and local law enforcement to share critical information, such as criminal background checks and warrants.
The news followed a week of outages affecting multiple agencies, such as the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the National Security Agency (NSA) and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).
The FAA incident, which officials said was prompted by a router installed while updating old telecommunication equipment to modern technology, led to a rare, hours-long ground stop on Friday, November 13th, as air traffic controllers struggled to communicate with planes in the air.
On Tuesday, an internal classified computer network used by the NSA reportedly experienced technical problems, though the issue has since been resolved, reports said.
Officials maintained that there was no indication that the FAA and NSA outages were part of a cyber-attack.
Anonymous USDA sources said that a program the agency uses to send payments to farmers was targeted by a cyber-attack, raising concerns that — though no other systems were targeted — hackers could possibly access sensitive information through the breach.

sources.text:
Trump says ‘maybe we’ll learn things’ after FBI is hacked again: ‘I always like to put things in a positive spin’
‘Maybe we’ll learn about voter fraud,’ the president told Fox News after yet another hacking incident
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article

Already a member? Log in
After the Federal Bureau of Investigation was hacked for the second time in recent months, President Donald Trump said “maybe we’ll learn things.”
Speaking by phone to Fox News on Saturday morning, Trump addressed new reporting that the FBI’s National Crime Information Center appeared to have been breached.
The reported hack would mark the second intrusion into an FBI system since September. The alleged hack also follows a string of high-profile technology disruptions affecting Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and air traffic control systems, among many others.
“Well, we just heard about it, and I will say it’s not good. I don’t like that,” Trump told his former White House press secretary and Fox News personality Kayleigh McEnany. “But maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise.”
The 80-year-old president then ticked through a list of what he called “hoaxes,” referring to claims of Russian interference in the 2016 election and his 2019 impeachment over allegations he pressured Ukraine to investigate Joe Biden.
“Because you know you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax. You had all of these other hoax,” Trump said. “We call it Ukraine. The Ukraine, Ukraine, Ukraine hoax. I was, you know the perfect phone call as they say.”
“You have so many other things, and maybe we’ll learn about them,” he continued. “Maybe we’ll learn about voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place.”
The president has long claimed that widespread voter fraud plagues U.S. elections and that the 2020 election was “rigged” as a result. Multiple investigations have failed to substantiate those claims, which officials in his own administration also rejected.
“And so I always like to put things in a positive spin,” Trump added.
The suspected breach, first reported by CNN on Friday, targeted a nationwide database that allows federal, state and local law enforcement agencies to share criminal justice information. The FBI had not publicly confirmed the incident or responded to the outlet’s request for comment.
The hack, which the bureau learned about Thursday, came two months after the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen sensitive personal information about FBI employees and job applicants from the bureau’s recruitment website.
After the bureau learned of the suspected breach, FBI Director Kash Patel appeared on Fox News on Friday to tout the agency’s security safeguards.
“The FBI and the intelligence community is going to continuously monitor those activities for nefarious actors,” Patel said. “And when and if such an actor comes up, you can rest assured that this FBI is going to hunt them down.”
“We are staying ahead of the curve and making up for lost time,” he added.
The Trump administration has sought in recent days to reassure the public after a string of high-profile technology disruptions grounded flights, locked workers out of their email and left customers unable to access their bank accounts.
The White House and top administration officials have said there is no evidence they were caused by “malicious foreign cyberattacks” or artificial intelligence.
Last week, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller reportedly sidelined Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin after he told Fox News that super intelligence — Trump’s preferred term for AI — may have been to blame for the outages, citing “one guy who is very smart with tech.”

“Maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise,” Trump said in the Fox News interview. “Maybe we’ll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place. So I always like to put things on a positive spin.”
He did not indicate which election he was referring to, but Trump has recently hinted on social media that voter fraud may have accounted for Democrats’ wins in this year’s midterms, which gave them control of Congress and multiple states’ governments.
Trump said after the midterms that he accepted the results, but his latest Fox News comments suggest that voters can’t yet be relieved of the president’s false notions that some elections may have been stolen.

sources.text:
Donald Trump suggested Saturday that an apparent FBI hack could reveal information about the Russia investigation, his first impeachment and alleged voter fraud, even as federal authorities investigate a suspected intrusion into one of the nation’s most important law enforcement databases.
During a telephone interview with Fox News host Kayleigh McEnany, Trump acknowledged that the reported cybersecurity breach was troubling but quickly shifted his attention to investigations involving his political career.
“We just heard about it, and I will say that it’s not good,” Trump said, before suggesting the incident might uncover information that had not previously been made public.
The political news that affects your wallet, your rights and your vote, broken down in plain language. Free in your inbox.
Trump specifically referenced the federal investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election, his impeachment involving Ukraine and his longstanding allegations of widespread voter fraud.
“Maybe we’ll learn about the voter fraud,” Trump said, suggesting the breach could expose information supporting allegations he has repeatedly made about American elections.
Trump did not provide evidence connecting the apparent FBI hack to any of those investigations or election-related allegations. There has been no public confirmation that the suspected intrusion involved records concerning Russia, Ukraine or voter fraud.
The remarks came as the FBI investigates a possible compromise of its National Crime Information Center, commonly known as NCIC, a nationwide database used by federal, state and local law enforcement agencies.
A person familiar with the investigation confirmed Saturday that the FBI was examining an apparent intrusion into the system. CNN first reported the incident Friday, citing sources briefed on the matter.
The NCIC contains information about wanted individuals, missing persons, stolen property, criminal histories and other records that officers use during investigations and routine law enforcement activities.
The database is particularly important because police departments across the country rely on its information to identify individuals with outstanding warrants, locate missing people and determine whether someone or something is connected to a criminal investigation.
The full extent of the suspected breach remains unclear. Authorities have not publicly identified who may have accessed the system, what information was potentially exposed or whether any records were altered.
The FBI declined to comment on the reported incident, according to The Associated Press.
Trump’s suggestion that the intrusion could expose information about the Russia investigation also revisited one of the most disputed subjects of his political career.
U.S. intelligence agencies concluded that Russia interfered in the 2016 election. Special counsel Robert Mueller’s investigation documented Russian interference and numerous contacts between Russians and individuals associated with Trump’s campaign, but it did not establish that the campaign criminally conspired or coordinated with the Russian government.
Trump has repeatedly characterized the investigation as a politically motivated effort against him.
His reference to Ukraine appeared to concern his first impeachment in 2019, when the House of Representatives charged him with abuse of power and obstruction of Congress following allegations that he pressured Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to announce investigations involving Joe Biden. The Senate acquitted Trump in February 2020.
Trump also returned to allegations of widespread voter fraud, a subject he has repeatedly raised while challenging election outcomes.
Following the 2020 presidential election, state election officials, courts and federal authorities found no evidence of widespread fraud sufficient to change the outcome. Trump’s own attorney general at the time, William Barr, said the Justice Department had not uncovered fraud on a scale that would have changed the result.
During Saturday’s interview, Trump did not identify a specific election or explain how information stored in the NCIC would substantiate his allegations.
The apparent FBI intrusion follows other cybersecurity incidents involving the bureau.
In September, the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for compromising an FBI recruitment website and obtaining information involving bureau employees and job applicants. The FBI also disclosed suspicious activity earlier this year involving an internal system containing sensitive investigative and surveillance information.
The latest incident comes amid heightened concerns about technology disruptions affecting federal agencies and major private companies. However, authorities have not established that the NCIC incident is connected to those outages.
For law enforcement agencies, a central concern is whether the suspected breach could affect the confidentiality or accuracy of information officers depend on every day.
Unauthorized access to sensitive records could potentially expose personal information or investigative details. Altered or unreliable records could also create problems for officers conducting background checks, verifying warrants or responding to emergencies.
Those remain potential risks rather than confirmed consequences of this incident.
The FBI investigation is expected to focus on determining how the apparent intrusion occurred, identifying the responsible parties and establishing whether sensitive information was accessed or compromised.
As of Saturday, federal authorities had not publicly disclosed those findings, leaving Trump’s suggestion that the hack could reveal information about his past investigations or voter fraud unsupported by any publicly verified evidence.
